When one metal is combined with another at a surface, its chemical properties can change by two mechanisms. Strain arises because the atoms adopt interatomic distances different from those in their own bulk lattice (tensile when stretched, compressive when squeezed). The ligand effect arises from heterometallic bonding between an atom and neighbors of a different element. The two usually occur together, which makes them hard to separate experimentally. See [d-band model](/papers/topics/d-band-model/) and [Bimetallic surfaces](/papers/topics/bimetallic-surfaces/).

## A unified matrix-element picture (2004)

Kitchin, Nørskov, Barteau and Chen expressed both effects through a single tight-binding interatomic matrix element for d-d coupling, summed over all nearest neighbors of a surface atom. The identity of the neighbors (ligand effect) enters through element-specific d-orbital length scales, and strain enters through the interatomic distance to the fifth power. Both effects act by changing the d-band width, and their contributions are cumulative: tensile strain narrows the band and raises the d-band center, while strong bonding to the substrate broadens it and lowers the center. For Ni monolayers, strong Ni-W bonding outweighs more than 10% tensile strain on W(110), the two nearly cancel on Ru(0001), and strain dominates on Pt(111), with H2 adsorption energies following the resulting d-band centers ([Kitchin et al. 2004](/papers/kitchin2004a/)). Summary: [kitchin2004a](/papers/kitchin2004a/).

## Quantifying strain, ligand, charge transfer and resonance contributions (2024)

Huang, Wang, Kamanuru, Achenie, Kitchin and Xin kept the same tight-binding picture (hopping integrals set by d-orbital radii and interatomic distances) inside a theory-infused neural network and used Shapley values to split the d-band center shift of 12,165 fcc surface sites into separate contributions. Strain and ligand effects each average about 0.15 eV, charge transfer about 0.01 eV, and a band-shape resonance effect about 0.20 eV. For Pt monolayers on fcc(111) substrates strain dominates, and the strain and ligand contributions correlate linearly with the substrate's bulk lattice constant and d-orbital radius. A learned bond-length factor shows that relaxation partly counteracts imposed strain, with tensile systems contracting and compressive ones expanding ([Huang et al. 2024](/papers/huang2024/)). Summary: [huang2024](/papers/huang2024/).
